topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Systems interfaces often describe fields as bits, masks, and byte sequences. C++ provides tools for those representations, but signed arithmetic and object layout rules still apply. We will build checked bit masks, inspect an unsigned value’s bytes without violating aliasing rules, and distinguish the value’s mathematical bits from the order in which its bytes appear on one machine.

The actual problem is an undocumented representation contract: field width, byte order, valid values, and buffer boundaries were never specified.

topics.summary: Binary and hexadecimal are not different numeric types; they are different ways to write or display values. A hexadecimal digit corresponds to four binary bits, making hex convenient for masks and byte-oriented diagnostics. Integer literals can use binary or hexadecimal notation while still participating in ordinary type and conversion rules.

blocks.text: A C++ byte is the unit measured by sizeof; its bit count is described by CHAR_BIT. The network protocols in the later labs specify eight-bit octets and use a compile-time check for that assumption. Making the assumption explicit is more precise than saying that every conceivable C++ implementation must have eight-bit bytes. Similarly, exact-width integer typedefs exist only when the implementation supports the required representation.

topics.title: 2.1.2 Inspecting Raw Binary Representation
topics.summary: An object’s representation is the sequence of bytes that stores it, while its value is the meaning those bytes represent under the type. std::bit_cast can copy a representation between equal-sized trivially copyable types under its requirements. Character and byte access facilities also support inspecting object bytes, but arbitrary reinterpretation as an unrelated typed object can violate aliasing and lifetime rules.

blocks.text: Endianness describes byte ordering for multi-byte values. It does not change which numeric bit is selected by an unsigned shift. A portable protocol should encode byte order explicitly rather than dumping native representation. The example prints native bytes for observation but verifies only size and value-level mask behavior, not one assumed host byte order.

blocks.text: A diagnostic byte dump answers “what representation is present here?” It does not by itself answer “is this a valid packet?” For example, the mathematical value 0x01020304 might appear in memory with its least significant byte first or with its most significant byte first. A protocol can choose one order regardless of the host. The decoder should implement that choice rather than infer it from the machine running the decoder.

blocks.text: For a four-octet big-endian field, the bytes 01 02 03 04 represent 1 * 2^24 + 2 * 2^16 + 3 * 2^8 + 4. A little-endian field containing the same value uses the reverse byte sequence. These formulas define the format independently of native storage. Test a decoder against a known vector, not only against its own encoder: two components containing the same reversed-order mistake can pass a round-trip test.

blocks.text: A byte dump can also contain information that is not part of the object’s logical value. Padding bytes and implementation-specific layout make raw structure dumps unsuitable as a portable wire format. Pointers are especially inappropriate: their numerical representations do not give another process ownership of the pointed-to objects. Define fields, lengths, and encodings explicitly instead.

blocks.text: In a debugging notebook, label a dump with both its interpretation and its limits: “native representation of this unsigned value on this target,” or “four-octet big-endian length field from the protocol.” The former is an observation; the latter is a contract. Keeping those labels separate prevents an incidental machine layout from quietly becoming the specification that every future client must imitate.

topics.title: 2.2.1 Creating Bit Masks
topics.summary: A mask selects one or more bit positions. Shifting an unsigned one left by an index creates a single-bit mask when the index is smaller than the type’s width. A negative shift count or a count at least as large as the promoted operand width is invalid. Check a runtime bit index before shifting.

blocks.text: A single-bit mask is a value with exactly one selected position. Before computing it, establish the width of the operation and validate the index. For an unsigned 32-bit operation, position 31 is the last valid single-bit position; position 32 is not a request for an empty result. A runtime check must precede the shift. Checking the result afterward is too late if the expression itself had invalid behavior.

blocks.text: Named masks turn numerical positions into domain concepts. Suppose a status field assigns bit zero to enabled, bit two to dirty, and bit five to acknowledged. Define those names in one place. Code that tests dirty_mask communicates intent better than code that repeats 0x04 across parsing, logging, and business logic. Central definitions also make reserved positions visible during review.

blocks.text: Fields spanning several bits need a second contract: how a logical value is positioned and extracted. A three-bit mode at offset four occupies positions four through six. To encode a mode, first check that its value is within the accepted domain, then shift and combine it with the surrounding field. To replace an existing mode, clear those positions before inserting the new bits. Otherwise, old set bits can survive and produce a different mode.

blocks.text: Watch the boundary when constructing an all-ones mask. An expression such as (one << width) - one is not valid when width equals the full width of the promoted left operand. Handle the full-width case explicitly or use the type’s maximum value. A helper should state its accepted width interval and test zero, one, the last partial width, and full width according to that contract.

blocks.text: Reserved-bit policy is an application decision. A strict internal protocol might reject every unknown incoming bit to catch incompatible versions early. A forwarding gateway might preserve unknown bits without interpreting them. Neither policy should arise accidentally from a mask that silently discards information. Describe the policy, then test an input containing an otherwise-valid value plus one reserved bit. The test should demonstrate the chosen compatibility behavior, not simply that an integer was produced.

Watch the boundary when constructing an all-ones mask. An expression such as (one << width) - one is not valid when width equals the full width of the promoted left operand. Handle the full-width case explicitly or use the type’s maximum value. A helper should state its accepted width interval and test zero, one, the last partial width, and full width according to that contract.

Reserved-bit policy is an application decision. A strict internal protocol might reject every unknown incoming bit to catch incompatible versions early. A forwarding gateway might preserve unknown bits without interpreting them. Neither policy should arise accidentally from a mask that silently discards information. Describe the policy, then test an input containing an otherwise-valid value plus one reserved bit. The test should demonstrate the chosen compatibility behavior, not simply that an integer was produced.

reading.title: Guided lab — Design a small status-field codec
paragraphs: Define a one-octet teaching format with named flags, one small enumerated field, and at least one reserved bit. Write down whether unknown bits are rejected. Implement an encoder from domain values and a decoder returning either a valid structured result or an explicit error. Do not expose a partially decoded object as success.

Enumerate all 256 octet values on the eight-bit lab baseline. For each value, classify validity using a simple independent specification function. Compare the decoder’s decision and fields with that classification. For every valid domain value, verify encode/decode agreement, but keep the independently specified byte cases as well. A round trip and an external-vector test protect different contracts.

Add property checks for set, clear, and toggle. Setting a flag twice should be idempotent; clearing twice should also be idempotent; toggling twice should restore the original state. Test “any” and “all” with masks containing several bits. Include a zero mask and document whether the public API accepts it.

Extend the format with a four-octet length in a specified byte order. Test zero, one, 255, 256, and a value with four different octets. Reject truncated input before indexing. Do not allocate a payload merely because the decoded integer fits; a separate maximum-size policy belongs to the framing layer.

Review reasoning. Why can two wrong functions pass a round trip? They can share the same incorrect convention. Why validate before shifting? The invalid operation cannot be repaired by inspecting its result. Why are a mask and a domain type different? A mask describes representation; the domain type describes permitted meanings. Why is atomicity not covered by a single-thread test? It concerns interactions and ordering absent from this experiment.

Completion criterion. Produce the field specification, known vectors, validity enumeration, and exact failure policy. Those artifacts make the representation understandable to a second implementation rather than merely reversible by your own code.
